title: HTTP Header Field X-Frame-Options
summary: Describes the X-Frame-Options HTTP header, which a server uses to tell browsers whether its content may be displayed inside frames on other web pages. It was created to help defend against clickjacking.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a sign that says do not put my picture inside your poster, so tricksters cannot hide it under fake buttons.

subtitle: The HTTP header that lets a site forbid other pages from displaying it in a frame, as a defense against clickjacking.

tldr.problem: An attacker can layer a victim page invisibly beneath a decoy page so that a user's clicks land on buttons they never meant to press (clickjacking).
tldr.mechanism: A server sends the X-Frame-Options response header with exactly one of DENY, SAMEORIGIN or ALLOW-FROM, and the browser refuses to render the content in a frame that breaks that policy.
tldr.outcome: The RFC only documents what browsers already did, notes that implementations differ, and says the header is expected to be replaced by a Frame-Options directive in Content Security Policy 1.1.

facts.label: ALLOW-FROM origins
facts.value: One only; no wildcards or lists

today: RFC 7034 is an Informational document and is not marked obsoleted or updated. The text itself says the "X-" construction is deprecated (see RFC 6648) and that the header is expected to be replaced by a Frame-Options directive in Content Security Policy 1.1.

sections.title: Clickjacking and the Header
sections.content:
In 2009 and 2010 browser vendors introduced a non-standard HTTP header field, X-Frame-Options, to protect against clickjacking. In that attack, someone uses transparent or opaque layers to trick a user into clicking a button or link on a page from server B while intending to click the overlaying page from server A. The clicks are hijacked, possibly in an existing session on server B, so both the user and server B are attacked.

RFC 7034 is informational documentation of current use. It says earlier defenses such as frame-breaking JavaScript were shown to have weaknesses, and that short of disabling frames and scripts entirely, users are vulnerable. With the header, a page from host B declares that its content must not be displayed in a <frame> or <iframe> of another page, and the browser enforces it.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster puts a see-through sheet with a fake button on top of a real button. You think you press the fake one, but you press the real one underneath. The header lets the real page say do not let anyone put me underneath.

sections.title: The Three Values
sections.content:
The header must be set to exactly one of three mutually exclusive values.

  • DENY: the browser MUST NOT display the content in any frame.
  • SAMEORIGIN: the browser MUST NOT display it in a frame from a page of a different origin than the content itself. If the browser cannot reliably decide, it MUST treat the case as DENY.
  • ALLOW-FROM followed by a serialized origin: the browser MUST NOT display it in a frame from any page whose top-level browsing context has a different origin than the one named.

The value is defined in ABNF, so the keywords are case-insensitive. After ALLOW-FROM comes required whitespace, which SHOULD be generated as a single space. Anything after the "/" in the origin is ignored. Wildcards or lists of several domains in one ALLOW-FROM are not permitted. Examples from the RFC: X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://example.com/.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three signs. One says nobody may frame me. One says only my own website may. One says only this one named website may.

sections.title: Browser Behavior and Quirks
sections.content:
Browsers cover the main ways to embed HTML from other domains: the iframe, frame, object (requiring a redirect), applet and embed tags. Plugins that show HTML views like frames must follow the policy too. If the header prohibits framing, the browser MAY abort downloading or parsing at once. On a violation it SHOULD redirect to a "NOFRAME" page, and some browsers show a message that lets the user open the target in a new window while others simply render an empty frame.

Implementations vary. ALLOW-FROM began as an Internet Explorer extension and is not uniformly implemented. The known implementations judge SAMEORIGIN by the framed page and the top-level browsing context, while others might compare the framing page or the whole chain of nested frames. Current implementations also ignore the port when comparing origins, which conflicts with RFC 6454.

Because ALLOW-FROM takes only one origin, the RFC describes a pattern for several framers: the framing page passes its origin in a query string, the server checks it against a list, and returns that origin in the header only if it passes. The RFC also recommends against caching the header, since a response may differ per request, and notes that none of the major browsers it lists cache it.
sections.plainLanguage: Different browsers read the sign slightly differently. Some show a polite note when a frame is blocked and some just show an empty box.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has placed X-Frame-Options in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, using the procedures of RFC 3864. The registration lists the applicable protocol as http, the status as Informational, the change controller as IETF, and this document, RFC 7034, as the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The header's name was written in the official list of header names so nobody else reuses it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The header improves protection against clickjacking but is not self-sufficient. It must be used with other measures such as secure coding (input validation, output encoding) and Content Security Policy 1.0.

Current implementations do not check the whole ancestor chain of frames. If a resource from origin A embeds untrusted content from origin B, that content can embed another resource from A that has SAMEORIGIN, and the check passes when only the top-level context is verified. Embedding other sites' content can therefore leave a page open to clickjacking even with the header. The header must be sent as a real HTTP header; it is explicitly ignored when declared in a meta http-equiv tag.

On privacy, ALLOW-FROM lets a server infer which page is framing it and discloses the origin named in the header. The RFC recommends generating the header per request with the design pattern above to reduce this.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign helps, but it is not a magic shield. If you let a stranger put things inside your page, they can still sneak around the rule.

items.label: No framing
items.desc: Never display the content in any frame.

items.label: Same origin only
items.desc: Display only in frames from a page of the same origin; treat as DENY if unsure.

items.label: One named origin
items.desc: Display only when the top-level page has the serialized origin given after the keyword.
